pressure-ratings.title: ASME B16.5-2025 pressure ratings by material group
pressure-ratings.metaDescription: ASME B16.5-2025 pressure–temperature ratings in bar (SI) for Group 1.1 plus 12 common alloy and stainless steel groups, 1.5 to 2.6.
intro: Tables 2-1.1 (SI units, bar) and 2-1.1C (U.S. Customary units, psig) of ASME B16.5-2025 give the maximum allowable working gage pressure for Group 1.1 flanges in Classes 150, 300, 400, 600, 900, 1500 and 2500. Group 1.1 is the carbon, carbon-manganese and low-nickel steel family. The SI table runs from 38 °C to 538 °C and the U.S. Customary table from 100 °F to 1,000 °F. The 2025 edition is a technical revision, not a reprint: its change record lists the rating tables as revised, so a rating taken from a 2017 or 2020 table should be re-read before it is reused.

A table is read by material, class and design temperature. The first row is a floor rather than an extra data point — at any temperature at or below 38 °C (100 °F) the 38 °C / 100 °F rating applies (para. 2.4). Linear interpolation is allowed between the listed temperatures. Interpolation between pressure classes is not, because each class is a separate rating curve, and values must not be extrapolated above the highest tabulated temperature. The SI and U.S. Customary tables are separate prints of the same ratings: para. 1.6 makes each system of units independent and states that the values are not exact equivalents, so convert only for information.

The page reproduces the complete Group 1.1 grids in both unit systems, preceded by the five material rows they apply to, and then the SI (bar) ratings for twelve further groups that cover most alloy and stainless steel flanges: Groups 1.5, 1.9, 1.10, 1.14, 1.15 and 1.17 (carbon-molybdenum, chromium-molybdenum, 9Cr and 9Cr-Mo-V steels) and Groups 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 2.4, 2.5 and 2.6 (the 304, 316/317, 316L/304L, 321, 347/348 and 309H austenitic stainless families). The notes under each table carry the real service limits — graphite conversion, killed or normalized-and-tempered material, minimum carbon content, heat-treatment conditions and the pointer to para. 2.5.3 for minimum temperatures.

Only SI ratings are transcribed for the groups other than 1.1, and the U.S. Customary companion tables 2-1.5C to 2-2.6C are not repeated here. The remaining groups (1.2–1.4, 1.7, 1.11, 1.13, 1.18, 2.7–2.13 and 3.1–3.19) are also still only in the standard. A group number fixes the rating curve: a Group 2.3 forging is not rated from the Group 2.2 table even though both are 316-type steels.

sections.heading: Materials the two tables apply to
paragraphs: Both tables name the same five material rows and the same accepted specifications. A flange made to one of these forgings, castings or plates is rated from Table 2-1.1 / 2-1.1C, provided the design temperature is inside the limit in the note marked against that row.

sections.heading: Applying a rating to a flange
bullets: Find the flange material group in Table 1.1-1. A105, A216 WCB, A515 Gr. 70, A350 LF2, A516 Gr. 70, A537 Cl. 1, A350 LF6 Cl. 1 and A350 LF3 are all Group 1.1, so all of them use Tables 2-1.1 / 2-1.1C.
Use the design metal temperature, not the fluid temperature. The rating temperature is that of the pressure-containing shell (para. 2.4).
At or below 38 °C (100 °F) take the first row; do not read the floor as a limit on how cold the part may run — the minimum-temperature rules are separate (note 6, para. 2.5.3).
Interpolate linearly between the two temperatures that bracket the design temperature, in the table for the unit system you are working in. Do not interpolate between classes.

Check the row note before using a hot rating: note (3) limits A350 LF6 Cl. 1 and A516 Gr. 70, note (4) limits A537 Cl. 1, note (5) limits A350 LF3, and note (2) requires killed steel above 455 °C (850 °F).

The flange rating is one input to the joint design. The governing piping code may impose lower limits for the same material, and a mixed joint is rated at the lower of the two flange ratings (para. 2.3.2).

sections.heading: U.S. Customary tables and the groups not reproduced here
paragraphs: ASME B16.5-2025 prints a U.S. Customary companion table for every rating table — 2-1.5C through 2-2.6C for the groups on this page — and each is printed next to its SI table. Those psig tables are not reproduced here because the values are independent prints of the same ratings, not conversions of the bar values: use the table for the unit system you are working in (para. 1.6).

The group 1.1 U.S. Customary table (2-1.1C) is reproduced above because Group 1.1 is the one group shown in both unit systems. Groups 2.7–2.13 and 3.1–3.19, and all U.S. Customary tables other than 2-1.1C, are still only in the standard. The purchased 2025 edition governs.

faq.q: Are these the revised 2025 ratings or values carried over from 2020?
faq.a: These are transcribed cell by cell from Tables 2-1.1 and 2-1.1C of the 2025 edition. The 2025 Summary of Changes records the pressure–temperature rating tables as revised after the ceiling values in Nonmandatory Appendix A, Tables A-1 and A-2 were changed. A value copied from a 2017 or 2020 table is therefore not automatically valid for the 2025 edition and should be re-read.

faq.q: What is the allowable pressure of a Class 150 Group 1.1 flange at 20 °C?
faq.a: 19.6 bar (285 psig). The first row of each table — "min. to 38 °C" / "min. to 100 °F" — covers every temperature at or below 38 °C (100 °F), so a lower ambient temperature does not increase the rating (para. 2.4).

faq.q: Why do the bar and psig values not convert exactly into each other?
faq.a: ASME B16.5 states the two unit systems as independent standards and says the values are not exact equivalents (para. 1.6). Convert only when a number must be understood in the other system; do not mix SI and U.S. Customary values in the same calculation or on the same datasheet, which the standard treats as nonconformance.

faq.q: Can the table be extrapolated above 538 °C (1,000 °F)?
faq.a: No. 538 °C (1,000 °F) is the highest tabulated temperature for Group 1.1 and the standard permits interpolation only between the listed temperatures. Group 1.1 carbon steels are also limited below that temperature by the row notes, for example A350 LF3 at 343 °C and A350 LF6 Cl. 1 at 260 °C.

faq.q: Which material group is A182 F316L?
faq.a: Group 2.3. Table 1.1-1 lists A182 Gr. F316L, A240 Gr. 316L and A182 Gr. F317L under Group 2.3, so the rating is read from Table 2-2.3 — not from Table 2-2.2, which holds F316 and F316H. The 2-2.3 table stops at 454 °C because note (1) limits every specification in the group to that temperature.

faq.q: Can a Group 2.2 flange use Group 2.1 ratings?
faq.a: No. A rating belongs to the material group printed against the grade in Table 1.1-1, and each group is tabulated separately because the allowable stresses differ. F316 and F316H are Group 2.2 and are read from Table 2-2.2; F304 and F304H are Group 2.1 and are read from Table 2-2.1. A joint that mixes two groups is rated at the lower of the two flange ratings (para. 2.3.2).

material-groups.title: ASME B16.5-2025 material groups and bolting tables
material-groups.metaDescription: All 116 rows of ASME B16.5-2025 Table 1.1-1 by material group, plus the four bolting categories of Table 1.1-2 and Table 1.1-3.
intro: Table 1.1-1 is the master material list of ASME B16.5-2025. For every accepted material it gives four things: the material group number used by the pressure–temperature tables, the nominal chemical designation, the rating table that governs the group, and the ASTM specifications accepted for forgings, castings and plates. The table runs from Group 1.1 to Group 3.19 across printed pages 5 to 7 — 116 rows in this edition, because many groups accept several specifications for the same nominal designation.

The group number is the link between the material tables and the rating tables. A Group 1.1 flange is rated from Tables 2-1.1 / 2-1.1C, a Group 2.13 flange from 2-2.13 / 2-2.13C, and so on; the C-suffixed table is the U.S. Customary companion of the SI table. Group 1 covers carbon, carbon-manganese and low-alloy steels, Group 2 the stainless and duplex steels, and Group 3 the nickel and special alloys. Plate materials are restricted to blind flanges and reducing flanges without hubs (para. 5.1 and General Note (b)).

Two companion tables complete the material section. Table 1.1-2 lists recommended bolting in four strength categories — high strength, intermediate strength, low strength, and nickel and special alloy — with a notes column that carries grade-specific limits. Table 1.1-3 recommends bolt, stud, nut and thread standards for carbon and alloy steel bolting. The 2025 edition revised Table 1.1-1 and Table 1.1-2 (adding A320 L7M, B511, B572 and B637 bolting), so the lists below are the current ones.

sections.heading: How to read Table 1.1-1
bullets: Column 1 is the material group number. It is the index used throughout Section 2 of the standard, not a quality or strength ranking. The numbering is not consecutive: Groups 1.6, 1.8, 1.12, 1.16 and 3.18 do not appear in the 2025 table.
Column 2 is a nominal chemical designation (C-Si, 16Cr-12Ni-2Mo, 67Ni-30Cu), not a trade name. The same designation can appear more than once when different product forms are accepted.

Column 3 names the pressure–temperature rating table for the group. Add a C for the U.S. Customary version: Group 2.13 is rated from Table 2-2.13 in SI units and Table 2-2.13C in U.S. Customary units.
Columns 4 to 6 list the ASTM specifications the standard accepts by product form. Where the standard prints an ellipsis the cell is shown here as "—".

Plate materials are listed only for blind flanges and reducing flanges without hubs; additional plate materials in ASME B16.34 may be used with the corresponding B16.34 Standard Class ratings (General Note (b)).

Materials to ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, Section II may be used in place of a listed ASTM specification where the ASME requirements are identical to or more stringent than the ASTM ones (Note (1) to Table 1.1-1).
Temperature limits belong to the rating tables, not to this list: General Note (a) sends the reader to the notes under Tables 2-1.1C through 2-3.17C.

paragraphs: The bolting table is printed as four parallel lists: high strength, intermediate strength, low strength, and nickel and special alloy. The number in each category heading is the note that applies to the whole category; the number in the notes column adds a grade-specific rule. A dash means no extra note is printed for that entry, so only the category note applies.

footnotes.text: Repair welding of bolting material is prohibited.
High-strength bolting: may be used with all listed flange materials and gaskets.
Intermediate-strength bolting: may be used with all listed materials and gaskets provided the user has verified that a sealed joint can be maintained under the rated working pressure and temperature.
Low-strength bolting: may be used with all listed materials but only in Class 150 and Class 300 joints (see para. 5.3.4 and Nonmandatory Appendix B for gasket recommendations).
Nickel and special alloy bolting: intended for use with comparable nickel and special alloy parts.
Austenitic stainless, carbide-solution-treated but not strain-hardened. Use ASTM A194 nuts of a compatible material.
Nuts may be machined from the same material or from a compatible grade of ASTM A194.
Maximum operating temperature is set at 260 °C (500 °F) unless the material is annealed, solution-annealed or hot-finished, because hard temper lowers design stress in the creep-rupture range.

Forging quality is not accepted unless the producer that last heats or works the parts tests them to the requirements of another permitted condition in the same specification and certifies final tensile, yield and elongation properties equal to or better than that condition.

Special alloy intended for high-temperature service with austenitic stainless steel.

sections.heading: What the four bolting categories mean
bullets: High strength (note 2): bolting with allowable stresses not less than those of ASTM A193 Grade B7. It may be used in any flanged joint (para. 5.3.2).

Intermediate strength (note 3): the listed bolting and other bolting of comparable strength. It may be used in any flanged joint provided the user verifies the ability to seat the gasket and keep the joint sealed (para. 5.3.3).

Low strength (note 4): bolting with a specified minimum yield strength of no more than 206 MPa (30 ksi). It is limited to Class 150 and Class 300 joints (para. 5.3.4) and calls for the gasket practice in para. 5.4.2 and Nonmandatory Appendix B.

Nickel and special alloy (note 5): bolting for use with comparable nickel and special alloy components; the grade-specific notes (7), (8) and (9) on nuts, operating temperature and forging quality apply.

General Note (a): bolting must not be used beyond the temperature limits of the governing code. General Note (b): ASME BPVC Section II bolting materials may be used where their requirements are identical to or more stringent than the ASTM specification.
The strength categories are defined by strength, not by the ASTM designation alone; a grade is listed here because it falls into the category, and the notes decide where it may be used.

faq.q: Which pressure–temperature table applies to my flange material?
faq.a: Look the material up in Table 1.1-1 and take the table number in the "pressure–temperature rating table" column. The same row also gives the accepted forging, casting and plate specifications, so the certificate and the rating table can be checked against one entry. The C-suffixed table is the U.S. Customary companion of the SI table.

faq.q: Can plate material be used for any B16.5 flange?
faq.a: No. Para. 5.1 and General Note (b) to Table 1.1-1 restrict plate and flat-bar materials to blind flanges and reducing flanges without hubs. Additional plate materials listed in ASME B16.34 may be used with the corresponding B16.34 Standard Class ratings.

faq.q: Which bolting counts as high strength, and where can it be used?
faq.a: High-strength bolting is the category whose allowable stresses are not less than those of ASTM A193 Grade B7; the listed entries are A193 B7 and B16, the A320 L7 series and L43, A354 BC and BD, and A540 B21 to B24. It may be used in any flanged joint. Intermediate strength adds the A193 and A320 austenitic grades, A320 L7M, A449 and A453 651/660, and requires the user to verify gasket seating and joint tightness; low strength is limited to Class 150 and Class 300. Check the category note before substituting.

faq.q: What changed in the 2025 edition in these tables?
faq.a: The 2025 edition revised Table 1.1-1 and Table 1.1-2. The bolting table gained ASTM A320 L7M (now listed under intermediate strength) and ASTM B511 (N08830), B572 (N06230) and B637 (N07740, N07718) under nickel and special alloy, and the table notes were revised and renumbered. Table 1.1-1 also carries the 2025 additions to the forging specifications and the new rating table for Material Group 2.13 duplex steels. Confirm any bolting or material certificate against the 2025 list rather than an older one.

tolerances.title: ASME B16.5-2025 flange tolerances (Section 7)
tolerances.metaDescription: Required tolerances from ASME B16.5-2025 Section 7: thickness, facings, hub length, bores, bolt circle and drilling limits for NPS ½–24 flanges.
intro: Section 7 of ASME B16.5-2025 sets the manufacturing and inspection tolerances for flanges and flanged fittings: centre-to-contact dimensions, facings, flange thickness, welding-end and hub dimensions, bores and counterbores, and drilling. The standard prints metric values first with the inch values in parentheses; the tables below carry both, exactly as the limits are printed.

The tolerances are conformance limits, not process instructions. Section 7.1 says values are rounded per ASTM Practice E29 and that listing a decimal tolerance does not prescribe a measuring method, so the same limits apply whether a dimension is checked with a calliper, a micrometer or a CMM. Several limits are one-sided: flange thickness, for example, has a plus tolerance and a zero minus tolerance, and the hub at the welding end has a steel floor of 87.5% of nominal pipe wall instead of ± limits.

Section 7 is one part of the acceptance picture. Ring-joint grooves are toleranced in Table 5 (Table 5C), facing roughness is in Section 6.4.5, and bolting bearing surfaces are controlled by Section 6.6. The tables below cover the whole of Section 7 — including 7.8 on drilling and facing, which continues onto printed page 15 — with the related finish rules listed separately.

sections.heading: Centre-to-contact, facing and thickness tolerances (7.2–7.4)
paragraphs: These limits fix the relationship between the flange faces, the facing outside diameters and the flange thickness. They are read with the figures in Section 6: centre-to-contact and centre-to-end dimensions apply to fittings and to ring-joint flanges, while the facing diameters apply to raised faces and tongue-and-groove or female facings.

table.note: Metric values are printed first with the inch values in parentheses; both are reproduced. Plus and minus signs are as printed: where only a plus value is shown, no negative tolerance is permitted. The ring-joint groove is toleranced in Table 5 (Table 5C), not in Section 7.

Dimensions A, B and C refer to the figures in Section 6, and the dimension letters in the table should be matched against the figure for the flange type being inspected.

This is a floor, not a ± tolerance.

sections.heading: Drilling and facing tolerances (7.8)
paragraphs: Bolt-circle geometry is controlled in three separate ways: the diameter of the bolt circle, the centre-to-centre spacing of adjacent holes, and the concentricity of the bolt circle with the machined facing. The standard prints a single limit, not a ± tolerance, for concentricity.

table.note: The first two limits apply to all sizes. The concentricity limit is a single value in each size range; the standard prints no ± sign for it.

Bolt circle concentricity with machined facing

sections.heading: Rules that sit outside the tables
bullets: Rounding (7.1): for determining conformance, observed or calculated values are rounded to the nearest unit in the last right-hand digit used to express the limit, as defined in ASTM Practice E29. Listing a decimal tolerance does not imply a particular method of measurement.

Thickness (7.4): the plus tolerance is applied at the bolting bearing surfaces whether they are as-forged, as-cast, spot-faced or back-faced. Spot facing or back facing must not reduce the flange thickness below the tabulated minimum (para. 6.6) and follows MSS SP-9.
Hub thickness (7.5.4): the floor of 87.5% of nominal pipe wall overrides the plus/minus limits on dimensions A and B at the welding end.
Ring-joint grooves (7.3.1(d)): groove dimensions and tolerances are not in Section 7; they are tabulated in Table 5 (Table 5C).
Facing perpendicularity (7.3.2): the flange face must be square to the bore within 1° up to NPS 5 and within 0.5° from NPS 6.
Application: Section 7 limits the manufactured product. Pipe-end tolerances come from the pipe standards, and a flange that passes these limits can still be outside a piping code requirement.

sections.heading: Facing finish that goes with the tolerances (6.4.5–6.6)
paragraphs: Section 7 controls dimensions; the facing surface itself is controlled by the finish clauses in Section 6. These values are the ones an inspector will compare with a visual comparator, so they belong with the dimensional acceptance criteria even though they are printed in a different clause.
bullets: Tongue-and-groove and small male-and-female facings: gasket contact surface not rougher than 3.2 µm (125 µin.) (6.4.5.1).
Ring-joint grooves: side-wall finish of the gasket groove not rougher than 1.6 µm (63 µin.) (6.4.5.2).

Other facings: serrated concentric or serrated spiral finish with a resultant surface finish of 3.2 µm to 6.3 µm (125 to 250 µin.) average roughness; cutting tool radius about 1.5 mm (0.06 in.) or larger, and 1.8 to 2.2 grooves/mm (45 to 55 grooves/in.) (6.4.5.3).
Facing imperfections are limited by Table 3 (Table 3C); adjacent imperfections must be separated by at least four times the maximum radial projection (6.4.6).
Bolting bearing surfaces must be parallel to the flange face within 1° (6.6).

faq.q: Is there a minus tolerance on B16.5 flange thickness?
faq.a: No. Para. 7.4 gives +3.0/−0.0 mm (+0.12/−0.00 in.) for NPS 18 and smaller and +5.0/−0.0 mm (+0.20/−0.00 in.) for NPS 20 and larger. Thickness may exceed nominal but must not fall below it, and the plus tolerance applies at the bolting bearing surfaces whether they are as-forged, as-cast, spot-faced or back-faced.

faq.q: What tolerance applies to the bolt circle and bolt holes?
faq.a: Bolt circle diameter: ±1.5 mm (±0.06 in.) for all sizes (7.8.1). Centre-to-centre of adjacent bolt holes: ±0.8 mm (±0.03 in.) (7.8.2). Concentricity of the bolt circle with the machined facing: 0.8 mm (0.03 in.) up to NPS 2½ and 1.5 mm (0.06 in.) from NPS 3 (7.8.3).

faq.q: How tight is the hub length on a welding-neck flange?
faq.a: Length through hub: ±1.5 mm (±0.06 in.) up to NPS 4, +1.5/−3.0 mm (+0.06/−0.12 in.) from NPS 5 to NPS 10, and +3.0/−5.0 mm (+0.12/−0.20 in.) for NPS 12 and larger (7.6). Separately, the hub thickness at the welding end must be at least 87.5% of nominal pipe wall (7.5.4).

faq.q: Does Section 7 also control the facing finish?
faq.a: Not directly: Section 7 controls dimensions such as facing outside diameters and perpendicularity. Facing roughness is set by Section 6.4.5 — for example a maximum 3.2 µm (125 µin.) on tongue-and-groove and small male-and-female gasket contacts, 1.6 µm (63 µin.) on ring-joint groove side walls, and a 3.2–6.3 µm (125–250 µin.) serrated finish for other facings.

marking.title: ASME B16.5-2025 marking requirements (Section 4)
marking.metaDescription: ASME B16.5-2025 marking rules: manufacturer, ASTM material with grade and melt number, class number, B16/B16.5 conformance mark, NPS and ring-groove R.
intro: Section 4 of ASME B16.5-2025 defines the identification markings that must be applied to flanges and flanged fittings. It starts from MSS SP-25, the standard marking system for valves, fittings and flanges, and then modifies it with a specific list of items: the manufacturer, the material, the pressure class, the conformance mark, the size and, for ring-joint flanges, the ring-groove number. The 2025 edition's Summary of Changes lists no Section 4 entry, so these are long-standing requirements rather than new 2025 text.

The material marking rule is the one buyers and inspectors most often get wrong. Cast flanges and flanged fittings carry the ASTM specification, the grade identification symbol and the melt number or melt identification. Plate flanges, forged flanges and flanged fittings carry the ASTM specification number and grade symbol only — no melt number is required. A manufacturer may add its own trade designation for the grade, provided the symbols cannot be confused, and a component that meets more than one listed specification or grade may carry more than one symbol.

Some marks are conditional and some are optional. The "B16" or "B16.5" designation is mandatory but the "ASME" prefix is not. Temperature marking is not required, and if it is applied it must be shown together with the corresponding tabulated pressure rating. A Case number goes on only when the component relies on an ASME Case. The requirements are set out below clause by clause, with the exemptions and options in a separate section.

sections.heading: Required identification markings
paragraphs: The table lists what the standard requires, clause by clause, in clause order except for the optional temperature marking (4.2.5), which is listed last because it is not mandatory. The standard does not prescribe a layout; 4.2.4 only says the conformance mark is preferably placed next to the class designation.

sections.heading: Notes, exemptions and what is optional
bullets: General rule (4.1): flanges and flanged fittings are marked as required in MSS SP-25, except as modified by §4.2. MSS SP-25 is the baseline; Section 4 adds and overrides.

Material marking is an assurance (4.2.2(e)): applying the ASTM specification number or trade designation is the manufacturer's assurance that the material complies with that specification or specifications, including when multiple certifications apply.

ASME Code substitution (footnote 2 to 4.2.2): an ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, Section II specification number may be substituted for an ASTM specification number where the ASME requirements are identical to or more stringent than the ASTM specification for the grade, class or type.

Multiple material marking (4.2.8): permitted at the manufacturer's option, not required. It applies to components meeting more than one specification or grade listed in Table 1.1-1, and the marking must follow BPVC Section II, Part D, Mandatory Appendix 7.

Temperature (4.2.5): no temperature marking is required. If one is applied, it must be paired with the corresponding tabulated pressure rating for the material — a bare temperature is not a valid mark.

Case number (4.2.9): required only when the component relies on and meets a Case. Section 1.10 adds that a Case may be used only when agreed by the purchaser and the manufacturer, and that when a Case has been agreed the marking must include the Case number. A Case number is not a routine mark and does not replace the class or conformance marks.
Reducing flanges (4.2.6): the size marking must identify the NPS of each opening, not only the larger opening, as required by paras. 3.2 and 3.3.
Ring-joint flanges (4.2.7): the R mark and groove number go on the edge (periphery) of the flange, so they remain visible with the flange bolted up.
No 2025 change: the 2025 edition's Summary of Changes and List of Changes contain no Section 4 entry, so marking requirements carry over from the previous edition.

sections.heading: What a marked flange looks like in practice
paragraphs: The standard does not prescribe the order or the method — characters may be cast, stamped or laser-marked, and the conformance mark is only required to be preferably next to the class number. The strings below are therefore illustrations of the required content, not a mandated layout.
bullets: Forged weld-neck flange, single material: [manufacturer trademark] A105 150 B16.5 NPS 6.
Cast flange, single material: [manufacturer trademark] A216 Gr. WCB [melt number] 150 B16.5 NPS 6.
Ring-joint flange: the same identification marks plus R and the ring-groove number on the edge — for example R followed by the groove number taken from Table 5 (Table 5C) for that size and class.
Multiple-certification flange: the extra specification or grade symbols are added next to the first, marked so that the combination cannot be misread.
Case component: "Case ##" is added when the component relies on an ASME Case agreed with the purchaser.

faq.q: Is the "ASME" prefix on the B16.5 mark required?
faq.a: No. Para. 4.2.4 requires the designation "B16" or "B16.5" to indicate conformance, preferably located next to the class designation, and states that the use of the prefix "ASME" is optional. Either form of the conformance mark is acceptable.

faq.q: What is the difference between marking a cast flange and a forged flange?
faq.a: Cast flanges and flanged fittings must carry the ASTM specification, the grade identification symbol and the melt number or melt identification. Plate flanges, forged flanges and flanged fittings must carry the ASTM specification number and the grade identification symbol, with no melt number required (4.2.2(a) and (b)).

faq.q: Can a flange carry more than one material marking?
faq.a: Yes, at the manufacturer's option, when the component meets the requirements of more than one specification or grade listed in Table 1.1-1. The marks must be placed so as to avoid confusion and follow ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, Section II, Part D, Mandatory Appendix 7 (4.2.8).

faq.q: Must the temperature be marked on a B16.5 flange?
faq.a: No. Temperature markings are not required. If a manufacturer does mark a temperature, it must be shown together with the corresponding tabulated pressure rating for the material (4.2.5), so a temperature alone is not an acceptable identification mark.

changes.title: ASME B16.5-2025: what changed from the 2020 edition
changes.metaDescription: How ASME B16.5-2025 differs from the 2020 edition: revised pressure–temperature ratings, new ASTM materials, hub geometry rules and a new Appendix G.
intro: ASME B16.5-2025 is the current edition of the American pipe-flange and flanged-fitting standard, covering NPS ½ through NPS 24 in Classes 150 to 1500 (Class 2500 runs to NPS 12). It is a revision of ASME B16.5-2020: the B16 Standards Committee and ASME approved it, ANSI approved it as an American National Standard on 10 April 2025, and it was issued on 30 May 2025. The next edition is scheduled for publication in 2028.

The 2025 edition is not a reprint with a new cover. Its Summary of Changes records revised pressure–temperature ratings across the rating tables, additions to the material and bolting specification lists, a revised bore ('B') dimension and a revised minimum-hub-height method in the flange dimension tables, new threaded-flange figures, a new nonmandatory appendix on minimum temperature limits, and new definitions of may, shall and should. A drawing, datasheet or certificate that quotes 2017 or 2020 values therefore needs checking rather than assuming.

This page summarises those changes from the 2025 edition's own front matter — the Foreword, the Summary of Changes and the List of Changes in Record Number Order. The revised tables themselves are not reproduced here, so no 2025 rating, material or dimension values are asserted; read the current edition for those.

sections.heading: Summary of Changes: what the 2025 edition changed
paragraphs: The headline is that the 2025 edition makes technical changes, not just editorial ones. The pressure–temperature ratings were recalculated after the rating ceilings in Nonmandatory Appendix A changed; the material and bolting specification lists grew; the bore ('B') dimension and the minimum-hub-height rule in the dimension tables were revised; and the threaded-flange figures changed. Around those sit new definitions, new guidance, a new appendix and updated references.

The committee's margin note ([25]) flags every changed location, and each entry carries an ASME record number. The table below regroups the page-by-page entries into the subjects a buyer actually works with, keeping the record numbers so each line can be traced to the List of Changes in Record Number Order (printed p. xix). 'C' tables are the U.S. Customary companions of the SI tables.

sections.heading: The Foreword's own summary of the 2025 revision
paragraphs: The Foreword ends with the committee's own short list of what the 2025 edition added. The Foreword (p. 11) records that various ASTM materials, a new appendix for determining minimum temperature limits, and definitions for may, shall and should were added; that the pressure–temperature ratings were revised after revised ceiling values were adopted in Nonmandatory Appendix A, Tables A‑1 and A‑2; and that various other revisions to variables were made. The same page states that ANSI approved ASME B16.5-2025 on 10 April 2025.
Read against the record-number list, that short paragraph resolves into the following:
bullets: Materials: 'various ASTM materials' added. The record list names ASTM B462 and B564 forgings (16‑1229), and bolting specifications A320 L7M, B511, B572 and B637 (22‑651).

Minimum temperature: a new appendix — Nonmandatory Appendix G, Low Temperature Applications — added for determining minimum temperature limits, with supporting guidance in the temperature and materials clauses (21‑1888).
Definitions: may, shall and should defined in new Clause 1.11, with Clauses 2.2, 5.3.5(a) and 6.1.1 aligned to the definitions (22‑2279).

Ratings: the pressure–temperature ratings revised after the ceiling pressures in Nonmandatory Appendix A, Tables A‑1 and A‑2 were revised (22‑2110), followed through into every rating table (23‑2509 and others). This is the headline change for buyers.
Variables: 'various revisions to variables' is the Foreword's catch-all and is not itemised there; the Summary of Changes and the record-number list are the detail behind it.
Dates: ANSI approval 10 April 2025; date of issuance 30 May 2025; next edition scheduled for 2028 (pp. 3 and 11).

sections.heading: What this means for a 2017 or 2020 drawing or datasheet
paragraphs: Not every line in the Summary of Changes affects what is bought. But several do, and they are worth a deliberate check rather than a quick glance at the cover.
bullets: Ratings: re-read the allowable pressure for each size, class, material group and design temperature from the 2025 tables. Do not carry over 2017 or 2020 numbers.

Materials and bolting: confirm that the ASTM specification named on the certificate appears in the 2025 Table 1.1‑1 or 1.1‑2 — especially nickel-alloy Groups 3.1, 3.6 and 3.12, and the newly added L7M and nickel-alloy bolts.
Geometry: re-check the B (bore) dimension, hub dimensions and minimum hub height in Tables 8 to 22, plus the threaded-flange figures, before machining or inspecting.

Installed equipment: the 2025 edition's §1.3 continues to recognise earlier-edition ratings for components already installed in accordance with them, except where a code or regulation governs. The edition named on the purchase order remains the reference an inspector will use.
Paperwork: update datasheets, ITPs and reference lists to 'ASME B16.5-2025'. On a purchase order, state the year — '2025' — not 'current edition'.

sections.heading: What this page covers, and what it does not
paragraphs: This page is based on the 2025 edition's front matter: the cover and title pages, the copyright page and contents (PDF pp. 1–4), the Foreword (PDF pp. 9–11), the committee roster and correspondence (PDF pp. 12–13), the Summary of Changes (PDF pp. 15–19), the List of Changes in Record Number Order (PDF p. 20) and printed page 1 of the standard text (PDF p. 22). Printed page 1 of the standard is PDF page 22, so printed and PDF page numbers differ from that point onward.

It does not contain the revised pressure–temperature tables, the material and bolting tables, the dimension tables and figures, or Nonmandatory Appendix G. This page therefore describes what changed and why it matters, but reproduces no 2025 rating, material or dimensional value. For those, use the purchased ASME B16.5-2025 edition; where a purchase specification names an edition, that edition governs.
Where the committee's own text leaves a point open — for example the 'various revisions to variables' in the Foreword — we say so rather than guess.

faq.q: Do I need to re-check ratings when moving from B16.5-2020 to B16.5-2025?
faq.a: Yes. The 2025 edition revised the pressure–temperature ratings in Tables 2‑1.1 through 2‑3.19 (and the C tables) after the rating ceilings in Nonmandatory Appendix A, Tables A‑1 and A‑2 changed. Any allowable pressure taken from a 2020 or 2017 table should be re-read from the 2025 edition before it is used in a design, datasheet or quotation. The revised tables are not reproduced here, so this page does not list the new values.

faq.q: Did the flange dimensions change in 2025?
faq.a: Yes, in places. The Summary of Changes records a revised 'B' (bore) dimension for slip-on, socket-welding, welding-neck and lapped flanges, a revised minimum-hub-height method with hub height H added to Figures 7 and 8, new threaded-flange figures (threads to the face on Class 150; a counterbore on Class 300), and errata corrections to individual values — NPS 14 outside diameter 553 to 533, NPS 20 outside diameter 693 to 698, and the Class 2500 NPS 2½ ring-joint groove depth 9.522 to 9.53. The 2025 edition should not be treated as purely editorial; the revised tables are needed for the new values.

faq.q: What are the new minimum-temperature limits?
faq.a: The 2025 edition adds a nonmandatory appendix for determining minimum temperature limits — Nonmandatory Appendix G, Low Temperature Applications — and adds guidance in Clauses 2.4, 2.5.3, 5.1.2 and 5.3.4. The Foreword and the record list describe it as a determination method, and the contents also list a table of example minimum use temperatures. Neither the appendix nor that table is reproduced here, so we cannot quote limits here; use the current edition to establish the minimum temperature for the specific material and grade.

faq.q: Which materials were added or removed?
faq.a: The Summary of Changes records additions and errata corrections, but no material removals. Added: ASTM B462 and ASTM B564 forging specifications; bolting specifications ASTM A320 L7M, ASTM B511 (N08830), ASTM B572 (N06230) and ASTM B637 (N07740 and N07718); and a new rating table (2‑2.13 / 2‑2.13C) for Material Group 2.13 duplex materials. Some nickel-alloy specification entries were also corrected by errata. The full lists are in the current edition.
